metadata.title: Neder v. United States, 527 U.S. 1 (1999) (No. 97-1985)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Neder v. United States

Opinion filed: 1999-06-10

Docket No.: 97-1985

Citations:
• 144 L. Ed. 2d 35
• 119 S. Ct. 1827
• 527 U.S. 1
• 1999 U.S. LEXIS 4007

Case holding summaries:
• holding that the failure to submit an element to the jury was harmless because the "defendant did not, and apparently could not, bring forth facts contesting the omitted element"
• holding that failure to submit an element to the jury is trial error subject to harmless error review
• noting that, under harmless error review, errors should be disregarded where "it appears beyond a reasonable doubt that the error complained of did not con- tribute to the verdict obtained" (internal quotation marks omitted)
• explaining that "most constitutional errors can be harmless"
• noting that where Congress uses terms with settled meanings, "a court must infer, unless the statute otherwise dictates, that Congress means to incorporate the established meaning of these terms" (internal quotation marks omitted)
• applying the same definition when judicially imposing a materiality requirement under federal fraud statutes
• applying harmless error analysis, rather than structural error, where jury was not instructed on one element of the offense
• discussing scope of harmless-error review of constitutional errors
• noting that, in cases where defendant failed to object to jury instruction, issue is reviewed for plain error
• this Court ordinarily leaves it to lower courts to pass on the harmlessness of error in the first instance
• failure to charge on an element of a crime was not prejudicial where uncontroverted evidence established an element of the offense and no reasonable jury could have concluded that the element had not been established beyond a reasonable doubt
• the term “actionable ‘fraud’” is one with “a well-settled meaning at common law”
• applying harmless error analysis to failure to submit issue of materiality to jury
• "`scheme or artifice to defraud'"
• listing examples of structural error
• concluding that failure to include element of offense in jury instruction is not structural error because it “does not necessarily render a criminal trial fundamentally unfair or unreliable vehicle for determining guilt or innocence”
• stating that erroneous admission or exclusion of evidence in violation of Fifth or Sixth Amendment rights is subject to a harmless error inquiry that asks "Is it clear beyond a reasonable doubt that a rational jury would have found the defendant guilty absent the error?"
• listing constitutional errors that are considered structural and thus defy analysis by harmless error standards and require automatic reversal
• relying on “ ‘natural tendency to influence’ ” standard and citing Restatement (Second) of Torts §538 definition of materiality
• describing structural error as “categorical”
• using this definition to interpret the mail, bank, and wire fraud statutes
• "The court . . . subsequently found, outside the presence of the jury, that the evidence established the materiality of all the false statements at issue."
• holding that failure to instruct the jury on a single element of the offense is reviewable for harmless error because the error "did not vitiat[e] all the jury's findings"
• “If, at the end of that examination, the court cannot conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that the jury verdict would have been the same absent the error – for example, where the defendant…raised evidence sufficient to support a contrary finding – it should not find the error harmless.”
• holding that omission of an element of a crime from a jury instruction is harmless error if the record does not contain sufficient evidence to support a finding that the element was absent
• holding that materiality is an element of bank fraud
• stating that constitutional error must be harmless beyond a reasonable doubt
• in assessing “whether the jury verdict would have been the same absent the error … a court, in typical appellate‐court fashion, asks whether the record Nos. 19‐1287, 19‐1768, & 19‐2049 19 contains evidence that could rationally lead to a contrary find‐ ing with respect to the omitted element”
• such errors including complete denial of counsel, biased trial judge, racial discrimination in selection of a grand jury, denial of self-representation at trial, denial of a public trial, and defective reasonable-doubt jury instruction
• "Accordingly, we hold that materiality of falsehood is an 8 UNITED STATES v. MORA element of the federal mail fraud, wire fraud, and bank fraud stat- utes."
• affirming convictions in spite of instructional error where the evidence made it clear beyond a reasonable doubt that a rational jury would have found defendants guilty even if properly instructed
• holding that failure to submit an element to the jury is trial error, subject to harmless error review
• erroneous jury instruction that omitted an element of the offense was subject to harmless-error analysis (quoting Johnson v. United States, 520 U.S. 461, 468 (1997))
• the error which occurs when an element of the crime charged is omitted from the jury instructions is subject to harmless error analysis
• "where a reviewing court concludes beyond a reasonable doubt that the omitted element was uncontested and supported by overwhelming evidence, such that the jury verdict would have been the same absent the error, the erroneous instruction is properly found to be harmless"
• listing constitutional errors that are considered structural and thus defy analysis by harmless error standards and require automatic reversal
• articulating test ‘‘for determining whether a constitutional error is harm- less’’ (emphasis added)
• noting that an instruction that omits an element of the offense "does not necessarily render a criminal trial fundamentally unfair or an unreliable vehicle for determining guilt or innocence." (emphasis in original)
• "[W]e have found an error to be `structural,' and thus subject to automatic reversal, only in a `very limited class of cases.'"
• “The omission of an element [from a jury instruction] is an error that is subject to harmless- error analysis.”
• finding error to be harmless “where a reviewing court concludes beyond a reasonable doubt that the omitted element was uncontested and supported by overwhelming evidence”
• harmless-error analysis applies when a district court’s jury instructions omit or misstate an element of an offense
• hold- ing that failure to instruct jury on essential element of offense is not structural error
• “The trial court, following existing law, ruled that the question of materiality was for the court, not the jury.”
• listing constitutional errors that are considered structural and thus defy analysis by harmless error standards and require automatic reversal
• “[T]he District Court instructed the jury that, to convict on the tax offenses, it ‘need not consider’ the materiality 27 of any false statements ‘even though that language is used in the indictment.’”
• courts must infer that Congress intended to incorporate settled meaning of terms it uses
• "where a reviewing court concludes beyond a reasonable doubt that the omitted element was uncontested and supported by overwhelming evidence, such that the jury verdict would have been the same absent the error, the erroneous instruction is properly found to be harmless"
• the error which occurs when an element of the crime charged is omitted from the jury instructions is subject to harmless error analysis
• holding that harmlessness test was met when the record evi- dence supporting the element was "so overwhelming" that the defen- dant had not even contested it
